about: The words of the chain reric_808 (Data/encounters/chain_reric_808_793.json; Design/content/chains/reric_808.md): King Godfred destroys the Wends' market of Reric in 808 and carries its merchants to Sliesthorp. Every title, intention, line and label key of its fourteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); the five news items the cards post; and one 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture. People: Dragomir, Asulf, the king (Godfred), Prince Thrasco, the count at Dorestad (Folcbert), Holmfast and the crewman Ravn are the spine's cast; Liuba (Dragomir's wife) and Ratimir (his sister's son) are ordinary invented people. Nothing is quoted: the Royal Frankish Annals for 808 to 811 are given in our own plain words. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: The wax booth

A Wend sits before a stack of wax cakes, each as big as a loaf and stamped with a thumb. He has a tally in his hand and a Saxon beside him to carry his words, and he has been watching your boat since she came in.
He says: sit. He says a man who stands before a Wend's booth is either buying or counting, and he would rather you were buying. His name is Dragomir. Mine does not matter. I am the mouth.
He says: this is his booth, the third from the water. His father's was the fifth. A family that moves two booths nearer the water in one lifetime is doing well enough.

He says: he is here for one moon with wax, because the Danes pay in silver and his own people pay in more wax. His booth is at Reric, on the Wends' shore, the third from the water. Any child there will show you.

He says: you come from where the iron is good. Axes, adzes, shears, knives that keep an edge. Our smiths make iron out of bog and it shows. Bring him tools from the Rhine and he will pay in wax and marten, and you may choose the skins yourself.

He says: your emperor has given our prince the Saxons' land beyond the Elbe. It is good land and it has not seen a plough for four years. He wants ploughshares, axes, sickles. He will pay in wax and marten, and you may choose the skins yourself.

He says: your emperor has also said that your merchants may come no nearer to us than Bardowick, and may bring no blades. He says a ploughshare is not a blade. He says also that a boat does not pass through Bardowick. He asks if he has understood your law.

He says: you will pay toll here to Prince Thrasco's man, and Thrasco's man sends a part of it over the water to the king of the Danes, so that the Danes go on thinking this beach is worth more to them whole. He says it has worked so far.
Take his order: six crates of Rhineland tools, brought to his booth at Reric
Buy three cakes of his wax now (75 d) and promise nothing
Buy nothing, eat at his table and learn ten words of his tongue

Dragomir cuts a notch in his tally and breaks the stick down its length. He keeps one half and gives you the other. Six crates of tools. He names no day: a Frisian comes when the wind lets him, he says, like weather.

Three cakes at twenty-five pennies, weighed on his scale and then on yours. The scales agree, which surprises both of you. The Saxon says his own people have a riddle about what the bees carry home from the groves, and gives it to you for nothing, since you bought.

Millet, smoked eel, honey in the comb and a sour drink you do not ask about. By the end you can say bread, salt, boat, wax, how much, too much, and four words the Saxon will not put into Frisian. Honey is cheap on this shore once the bees are taken, and he tells you when that is.
Iron for wax

Dragomir's booth is the third from the water at Reric: a sunk floor, a roof of reed, a stack of wax as high as a man's belt. He knows your boat before she grounds, and by the time you have her made fast his wife has set out bread and honey.
I have learned Danish since you saw me. It is easier than keeping a Saxon. I have my half of the stick. Have you the other half, and what goes with it?
The Frisian who buys nothing and remembers the way back. I have learned Danish since you saw me. It is easier than keeping a Saxon. Sit down.
My brother has land over the Elbe now, Saxon land. He cut the first furrow with a share made of bog iron and it bent like a wet reed. He has spoken of nothing else since.
A tenth of what you sell, for Prince Thrasco. Of that tenth a part goes over the water to the Dane. We pay a wolf to stay a dog. It is cheaper than a wall.

The Dane king lay at the Slie with all his ships and all his horses, the summer your emperor wanted to talk to him, and would not go and talk. A man who will not talk has decided something. I should like to know what.
We do not swear quickly here. A man who swears quickly has done it before. When we do swear we swear over water, because water goes everywhere and tells everyone.
Hand over six crates of tools for six cakes of wax and a timber of marten
Give him two crates as a guest's gift and ask no price
Tell him plainly you have brought no iron, and eat his bread

He tries every edge on his thumbnail and every axe on the doorpost, and is in no hurry. Then six cakes of wax and forty marten skins on a cord, and he lets you choose the skins as he said. The two halves of the tally go into the fire together. Among the Wends, he says, that means the next bargain needs no stick.

He looks at the two crates a long time. Then he fills a bowl from the bay, sets it between you, and says over it that your boat has a booth at Reric as long as his has a roof. His wife sends three crocks of honey down to the boat. He teaches you the words for what he swore, so that you know what you are held to.
He nods. 'A man who says he has nothing has at least that.' You eat his bread. Tools are still wanted on this beach, and still dear.
Ships called out

There are more hulls on the strand than the trade can account for, and the men tarring them are not shipmen: they hold the brush like a spear. Shields are stacked under a sail. Asulf the dealer is buying rope by the coil and paying without weighing twice.
Rope. A man in my trade never has enough rope in a year like this one. I will say no more than that. It would not be useful to me to say more.
You trade east, I think. You know the Wends' beach, the one with the wax. It is a good beach. I have always said it was a good beach.
A Frisian. Then you are the emperor's man, whether you know it or not. Sell your wine. Count your pennies. Do not count ships.
If you have bread or ale aboard, sell it today. A fleet eats like a fire. By the new moon they will be gone and you will be feeding it to pigs.
Stand Asulf a jar of ale (15 d) and ask where a man buys so much rope for
Ask the king's man to his face where the ships are bound
Ask nothing: an army eats, and you have things to sell

Asulf drinks slowly. 'The king goes against the Wends as soon as the hay is in. The Wilzi go with him for nothing: they have hated Thrasco's people longer than we have. There will be strongholds, and I will need the rope. And last of all the beach. The king says a market that pays him a part can pay him the whole, nearer home.' He puts the jar down. 'You did not hear it from me. You heard it from the ale.'

He laughs, which you had not expected. 'East. The Wends. Everyone on this strand knows it but the Wends.' Then he looks at you again. 'You trade on their beach. The king will want to know which booths are worth the carrying and which have a chest under the floor. A man could walk that beach before we come, and count. He would not be forgotten when the taking is shared.'

'Whose man asks?' Two of his fellows have come up behind you. It takes two ounces of silver, cut from your own purse and laid on his palm, to make you a wine seller again. But a man does not guard a secret so hard unless it lies near, and he looked east when he said it. East is the Wends, and the Wends have one beach worth the trouble.
Bread and ale are going at half as much again as they should, and nobody haggles. You sell and ask nothing. The ships are somebody else's business.
A word on the beach

Reric trades as it always has: wax, furs, people, pitch smoke, a Saxon quarrelling over a weight. Children are catching crabs under the boats. You are the only man on the beach who knows what the rope at the Danish landing is for.
You have a face like a man with a stone in his shoe. Sit. Eat first. Whatever it is will still be true after bread.
The Frisian. You look at my booth the way a man looks at a horse he has heard is sick. If you have something to say, say it in Danish. I have enough of it now.
A quiet summer. The toll is good. The Dane's part went over the water at the last full moon, as always, and his man took it and said nothing, as always.
If there is trouble it will come by land, from the Wilzi, as it does. The prince is watching the east. Nobody comes at Wends from the sea. What would they want? Wax?
Tell Dragomir alone, after dark, and let him do as he thinks best
Say it aloud before Thrasco's man and the whole beach
Walk the beach and count the booths for the king's man
Say nothing, sell out your cargo and be gone before the moon changes

He hears it through without moving. 'I cannot go. If I go, my neighbours ask why, and then the prince's man asks, and then I am the Wend who ran from a Frisian's story. But wax can go.' Before light, six cakes of his best wax and three cords of marten are under your boards. 'Sell it in the west. Keep the silver. If you are right I will need it. If you are wrong, bring it back and I will laugh at you every year until one of us is dead.'

Thrasco's man hears you out with his arms folded. It is an old woman who settles it, a seller of combs: she says the Dane's man took the toll at the full moon and did not count it, and a man who does not count what he is given expects to come back for the rest. Nobody laughs after that. For three nights boats go out loaded and come back light. The way behind the island is narrow and they show it to you, since you may need it too.

Thrasco's man says it loudly, for the beach: a Frisian is the Franks' man, the Franks want this trade at their own posts on the Elbe, and here is a Frisian with a tale to empty the beach. Men turn back to their scales. Only Dragomir comes to the boat after dark, with six cakes of wax and three cords of marten. 'I do not know if you are right. I know you had nothing to gain by saying it. Sell these in the west and keep the silver for me.'

Forty-one booths. Nine with a chest that has a lock. Eleven boats fit for the open sea. Two storehouses the prince's man keeps for the toll. You cut it on a stick in your own marks. Nobody asks why a Frisian walks so slowly. Dragomir's wife gives you a honey cake as you pass.
It is not your beach and they are not your people. You sell the last of the wine a little dear, because you are in no mood to haggle and it shows, and take the boat out on the morning wind.
Sails in the bay

At first light the bay is full of ships, more than you have seen in one water. There is no fight worth the name. By noon the king's men are going from booth to booth with a tally, and wax, furs, scales, looms, anvils and people are going down to the water. The king sits his horse on the rise behind the beach in a red cloak and watches it done. He does not come down.

Hear the king's word. This market is closed. The king has a better harbour for it, at the head of the Slie, and every merchant here is his guest there from today. You will load what is yours. What you cannot load will burn.
The king has had a part of this beach's toll for many years. He has thought about it, and he finds he would like all of it.
The Frisian with the stick. Forty-one, you said, and nine with locks. We found the nine. Load beside the king's ships, and stay near me.
A Frisian boat. The emperor's man on the Wends' beach. The king's word is for every merchant here. I did not hear him say 'except Frisians.'

They hanged Godelaib. A chief, taken by a trick and hanged like a thief. Thrasco is gone, nobody knows where. The Dane lost a brother's son at one of our strongholds, and he is making the beach pay for the boy.

The boats are behind the island, and the chests, and the old woman with the combs. There is nothing in my booth but a broken pot. Let him burn the pot. Come now, the way is narrow and the tide is going.
Take the king's peace: load where his men point and sail with the fleet
Slip the cable in the dark and row for the open bay
Say a Frisian is no Wend, and lay five ounces of silver (60 d) on the king's tally
Lie behind the island with the Wends' boats until the smoke is gone

You load. A king's man cuts a notch for your boat on the same stick as the Wends' boats, between a honey seller and a man with two looms. Behind you the reed roofs go up one after another, quickly, the way reed does. Nobody on the water looks back for long.

No moon, the ebb running, rags on the oar looms. A guard ship lies across the channel with a fire in a pot on her foredeck, and the men round the fire cannot see past it. You go by so close that you hear one of them say the Wends' ale is thin. By first light there is open water under you and smoke behind.

The guard ship is not where she lay at dusk. She is across the channel, and her men are awake. Somebody's spear shaft finds your ribs. The steersman takes four ounces of your silver, for the king's trouble, and sets you back in the line. 'You go to the Slie. Tonight or tomorrow. Tomorrow you keep your teeth.'

He weighs the silver in his hand, not on a scale, and looks up the rise. The red cloak does not move. 'The king gives the Frisian leave to go where he likes. The king says also: there is no market here now. When the Frisian wants wax, he will find it on the Slie.' The notch for your boat is cut off the stick with a knife.

Two days in the reeds with forty Wend boats, no fires, the children kept quiet with honey. On the second evening the smoke comes over the island, low and brown. On the third morning the bay is empty. The king has burned forty-one roofs and a broken pot, and has carried nobody to the Slie.

On the second day a Danish boat noses round the point, eight oars, looking for somewhere to water. She sees you before you see her. Her steersman looks at forty hidden hulls and then at the silver you are holding up. He takes the silver. He is a man with a farm, he says, not the king's dog, and he has seen nothing but reeds.
News from the east
A shipman in from the Baltic has news. He has told it four times today and is glad to tell it a fifth, with his hands.

This summer the king of the Danes went over the water against the Wends with all his ships. He took strongholds and hanged a chief, and he lost a brother's son doing it. And before he went home he burned the market at Reric to the sand.

He did not kill the merchants. He put them in the ships, with their scales and their wives, and set them down at the head of the Slie. He says it is their market now. A man steals a hive that way: he takes the bees and burns the tree.
Some got their goods out beforehand, they say. Sent them west in a stranger's boat. I should not like to be that stranger, or else I should like it very much. It depends on the stranger.
And he is building a wall. From the one sea to the other, they say, with one gate in it for carts. I have not seen it. I have seen the men digging.
And the Wends' prince is dead, Thrasco. He came back, and the Dane's men killed him on that same beach. So there was still something there to come back to.
Ask after a Wend named Dragomir, with a booth third from the water
Buy four cakes of wax from him (80 d), and do not ask whose it was
Hear him out and say nothing

'Third from the water? There is no third from the water. There is no water's edge with a booth on it.' He thinks. 'They are all at the Slie now, those that lived. Ask there. Ask for the Wends' strand. You will smell the wax.'
Twenty pennies the cake. Each has a thumb pressed into it, the way one man on that beach marked his wax. You do not look at the thumb for long.
You hear him out. Wax is cheap on the Slie this season, he says, with so much of it come in at once and so few of its owners in a state to haggle.
In the king's wake

The fleet goes north along the land in a long line: the king's ships, then the Wends' own boats rowed by their owners, low in the water with everything they have. The guard ships keep the outside of the line, like dogs.
Frisian! Close up. A gap in the line is a thing I have to explain, and I do not like explaining.

The ship with the shields turned inward. That is Reginold going home, the king's brother's son. He went first up a wall. The king liked him better than his own sons, they say. It is why the beach burned so thoroughly.
I know that guard ship. Her steersman is from my fjord. He counts well at noon and badly at dusk. I only mention it.

A sail astern, off the point. One of theirs. She has seen us, and she has twice our oars. There is shoal water to the south that would take us and not her. Or there may not be. It has been some years.
You there, the small boat! Every hull in these waters goes to the Slie this week. King's word. You seem to be going somewhere else.
Keep your place in the line
Drop astern at dusk, a boat's length at a time, and turn away with the dark
Run for it over the shoal water where she cannot follow
Heave to and say you are bound for the Slie like all the rest
You close up. The Wend in the boat ahead has a loom lashed across his thwarts and a goat standing in the bows. The goat looks at you all the way to the Slie.

A boat's length. Another. The guard ship's steersman counts the line at dusk and gets the number he wants. When the last light goes you put the helm over and let the land breeze take you. In the morning there is nobody on the water but gulls.

He counts better at dusk than Ravn remembered. The guard ship comes down on you under oars, and a spear stands in your planking a hand from the steersman's knee. It costs you a gift to have it called a mistake. She rows beside you from there to the Slie.

The shoal is where Ravn said it might be. You go over it with a hand's depth to spare and the lead going all the time. The guard ship stops at the edge like a horse at a ditch. Her steersman shouts something. The wind is the wrong way to hear it.

There is a shoal, but the tide is over it, and she comes across after you without slowing. Twice your oars. Her steersman takes four ounces for making him sweat and puts you in the line behind a boat full of looms. 'Next time, be a faster boat.'

You back the oars and wait for her. 'Bound for the Slie, like everyone. We lost the line in the dark.' He looks at your boat, which is too small to be worth his doubt. 'Then find it again. That way.' He has forgotten you before you have the sail up.
Set down

On the strand at Sliesthorp the king's men are pacing out plots with a knotted rope and driving hazel rods at the corners. The people of Reric sit on what they carried and wait to be told which rods are theirs. Up the slope, men with spades are standing in a line that runs out of sight to the west.

Each merchant has a plot, four rods by eight, with its short end to the water. Build on it before the frost and hold it over the winter and it is yours by the king's word. Leave it empty and it goes to a man who wants it.

The king is closing his border with a wall, from the eastern water to the western sea. One gate in it, for carts and riders. Every leader has his length to build, and every guest of the king owes days on it, or the price of a man's days.
So. You were right, and I am alive to say it. I will not ask about the wax today. A man who asks on the first day has already decided he was robbed.

I have a scale, a wife, and a tally with nothing to count. The Dane calls me his guest. In my tongue we have the same word for guest and for stranger. In his, I think, there is one for guest and cattle.
You were not there. Good. One fewer to feed on the way.

Not everyone from that shore came as a guest. Those taken at the strongholds are mine to sell. There is a boy in the pen, ten winters, who says his mother's brother is a merchant on this strand. They all say that. This one may be right.
Forty-one booths, I hear, and nine locks. That was neat work. The spokesman has not forgotten it. Nor have I. I like a man who counts.
Have a rod driven for yourself: a plot of the king's, and your days owed at the wall
Tell Dragomir his wax and furs are safe in the west and will come back to him as silver
Buy his sister's son out of Asulf's pen (90 d) and bring the boy to him
Go to the spokesman and ask what a count of forty-one booths is worth

Four hazel rods and a notch on the king's tally: a Frisian's plot between a honey seller's and a comb maker's. You owe six days at the wall, or a man to do them. Hold the plot over the winter and come back when the ice is out of the Slie.

He looks at you for the time it takes to count to ten. 'You came here to say it. You could have sailed past the mouth of the Slie and I would never have known whether the sea took you.' He asks for no oath. 'You came back. That is the oath.' Come again when the goods are sold, he says. He is not going anywhere.

Asulf names seven and a half ounces and does not say it twice. The rope comes off. The boy's name is Ratimir and he does not speak until he sees his uncle, and then he does not stop. Dragomir puts his hand on the boy's head and looks at you over it, and says nothing for some time. Come back in the spring, he says at last. He will have thought of what to say.

'When the taking is shared,' the spokesman says. 'After the wall is begun. Two moons. You will be called after the ships' leaders and before the cooks.' When you turn round, Dragomir is standing by his rods. He has seen whom you went to, and he has worked out the rest.
Word by merchants
The king's spokesman comes down to your boat himself, which he has not done before, and sends his men out of hearing. He has washed and put on a clean shirt. It is that kind of errand.
The border is shut and envoys do not cross it. Merchants do. A merchant can walk into a count's hall with a king's words in his head and nobody has to say that an envoy was received.

Say this at Dorestad, to the count, for the emperor. The king of the Danes has heard that the emperor is angry because he led his army against the Wends last summer. The king wishes to clear himself. It was the others who first broke the peace. Let counts from each side meet beyond the Elbe, at the border, and what was done wrong on either side be put right.
There is a piece of an arm-ring for the carrying. More, if an answer comes back by the same boat. The king remembers who is useful. He also remembers the other kind.
If you carry his words, carry six of mine. Tell the Franks: the Wends on the Slie are held, not settled. They gave our prince a sword once. Let them remember whose merchants these are.
Carry the king's word to the count at Dorestad, as it was said and no more
Carry the king's word, and Dragomir's with it: that the Wends on the Slie are held, not settled
Say you sell wine and are nobody's mouth
He has you say it back twice. Then a piece cut from a silver arm-ring, three ounces and a little, still warm from his arm. 'The count at Dorestad. Not his clerk.'

The spokesman has you say his words back twice and gives you a piece of an arm-ring for them. Dragomir gives you nothing and has you say his back once. Two messages in one head, and only one of them paid for.
'Then sell wine,' he says, and goes back up the strand. He will find another boat. With the border shut there is not much wine on the Slie this year, and what there is goes dear.
The count's hall

The count hears you standing, in the hall above the river, with a clerk at his elbow who writes on wax and does not look up. Through the door you can hear the toll being argued on the dam, as it is every day.
He sends me a wine seller. Not a kinsman with a white shield. A wine seller. So he wants to be heard and does not want to be seen asking.

It will go to the emperor. I think he will send counts to meet theirs, since it costs nothing, and I think nothing will come of it. A man who builds a wall first and asks to talk afterwards has finished talking.
And what did the merchant see, on the way to being given these words? A wall? How long? How many gates? Ships, drawn up or in the water? We have men who are paid to find out such things and do not.
'Held, not settled.' That is well said for a Wend. Thrasco is the emperor's friend and those are Thrasco's people. It will go in the same letter. I do not say anyone will ride for them.
Give the king's words as they were given, and nothing of your own
Give the words, and then everything you saw: the wall, the one gate, the ships on the strand
Say you were given words for the count and would as soon be rid of them: let the clerk have them, and go

You say it as it was said. The clerk's stylus stops when you stop. The count has five shillings counted out for you and tells the toll man that your boat is to be dealt with gently until Martinmas. 'A man who brings a message and adds nothing to it. I had heard there were such men.'

You tell it all: the turf wall and the men on it, the one gate, the plots on the strand, the hulls you counted without meaning to. The clerk fills three tablets. Ten shillings from the count's own purse, and the toll made light for half a year. As you go out the clerk is already reading it back to a man you do not know, and you think of how many people can read wax.
You say the words to the clerk in the doorway, once, quickly, the way a man puts down something heavy. The count does not get up. You are back at your boat before the tide turns.
The king's new town

A winter has gone over the rods on the strand. There are roofs between them now, a plank road down to the water, a jetty begun, and smoke from forty hearths that burned last year on another shore. Up the slope the wall is a green bank with a ditch before it, as far as you can see.
You held your plot. Not all did. The king said the first comers would be remembered, and I am the one who does his remembering.

A count's clerk at Dorestad has three tablets about our wall, I am told, and they are in your words. You may keep your plot. The king's word is the king's word. But a man does not get the king's gift for counting the king's ships.

So we are neighbours, Frisian. I did not choose my plot and you chose yours. It is the only difference between us, and it is a large one. Still, the wax sells. The Dane was right about the harbour. I hate him for that as well.
Six cakes of wax and three cords of marten went west in your boat. I see you have a plot and a new roof. I do not ask. I only count, and I am a patient man.
Thrasco is dead. He came back to our beach, to what was left, and the Dane's men killed him there. So there is nobody now to ask for us.

The king is dead, by one of his own house. Hemming his brother's son has the kingdom, and twelve of ours have sworn peace with twelve Franks on the Eider. The gate is open. The town stays where it is. A dead king's word still holds a plot.
Hold the plot by the king's word, free of the landing gift, as the first comers were promised
Build on the plot: a house and a store among the Wends' booths
Sell the plot to a Saxon who wants it more, and stay a guest

He says it before witnesses on the strand, which is how a thing is written here: the Frisian's boat owes no gift at this landing, by the king's word, while his house holds the plot. A winter's trade off the plot comes to three hundred pennies by weight and four cords of marten. At Dorestad they will say you are the Dane's man. For a year or two they will be right.

Oak posts, wattle, a reed roof, a store with a door that locks. Four hundred pennies by weight from the winter and eight cakes of wax owed you by neighbours who paid in what they had. A roof of your own on the Slie, on ground a king took from nobody in particular. At Dorestad they will say you are the Dane's man.

A Saxon with two sons pays seven hundred pennies by weight for four hazel rods and the right to stand between them. You keep a guest's seat at the landing and owe nobody days on a wall. Nobody in Frisia can say whose man you are, which in these years is worth something.
Faith kept

Dragomir has a roof on the Slie now, lower than the one that burned. He sets out bread and honey as he did at Reric, and talks of the weather, and does not ask the question he has waited two hundred days to ask.
Eat. I have told my wife every week that the Frisian will come. She has told me every week that the sea is wide and silver is heavy. One of us is about to be unbearable to live with.
The boy eats like a wolf and has learned to swear in Danish. My sister is alive. She walked eleven days to find out whether he was. You did that, and I have still not thought of what to say.

My kin's wax came round this autumn in Holmfast's boat, the Svea. He weighed it three times and charged me for two. So I have goods again, and a strand to sell them on, and no boat I would trust past the point.
I want a way home that does not go through the Dane's gate. A boat does not go through gates. You have a boat, and I have what goes in one.
He will not say it, so I will. We had nothing when they set us down. If we have something now it is because one stranger did what he said.
They killed Thrasco on our beach, the Dane's men, when he came back. I have no prince now. I have a partner, if he will have me. It is a smaller thing, and it is more use.
Count out the whole price of his goods (480 d) and take nothing for the carrying
Count out the price less a fair freight (360 d)
Say the boy was a gift, and ask what a Wend and a Frisian might carry together
Tell him the silver is not all there yet: give him your hand on it, and a year

Forty shillings, counted onto his table in fours. He weighs none of it. 'And the freight?' There is none. He is quiet. Then he fills a bowl with water and swears over it, slowly, as his people do when they mean it: half of what his boat carries is yours, half of what yours carries is his, for as long as both float. Eight cords of marten, ten cakes of wax and four sacks of amber go down to your boat as the first lading. His wife takes a ring of twisted silver from her temple and puts it in your hand. It was on her head when the beach burned.

Thirty shillings on the table and ten kept for the carrying. He nods: it is what he would have asked himself, and he says so. He swears partnership over a bowl of water, and five cords of marten and six cakes of wax go down to your boat. 'A fair man,' he tells his wife in his own tongue. You have enough of it now to know he said fair, and not more than fair.

'A gift.' He says the word in Danish and then in his own tongue, to hear whether it means the same in both. Then a bowl of water between you, and the oath: half of his lading yours, half of yours his, while both boats float. Four cords of marten and six cakes of wax go down to your boat that evening. The boy carries the wax and will not be helped.

He looks at your hand before he takes it. 'A year. I have waited two hundred days; I know how to do it now.' He will keep a corner of his store for your goods meanwhile. It is a kindness, and it is also a place where he can see them. His wife does not come out to see you off.
Reric holds

A Wend boat lies at the landing with new wax in her and a face you know at the steering oar. Dragomir has been asking for a Frisian boat at every beach for a month, and has a speech ready that he does not, in the end, make.
There. I told them: a small boat, a Frisian, a man who looks as if he is adding something up. They said that is every Frisian. But here you are.
You see? Third from the water. The posts are new and the reed is green, and the pot is mended. Sit. This time you will eat until you cannot stand.

He burned forty-one roofs. A roof is reed, and we have reed: the place is named for it. He found nine chests, as someone must have told him he would. There was sand in them. He stood on the rise a long time, they say. Then he went home.

I called you a tale-bearer in my heart, Frisian, before the old woman spoke. I say it aloud now so that it is not between us. The beach owes you. A beach pays slowly, but it does not forget where it stands.

The Dane knows a stranger warned us. He does not know which stranger. I would keep clear of his landing until he is tired of asking. Kings tire. Or they die. This one has many friends who would be glad of either.
They say he had plots marked out on the Slie for us, with rods. A whole strand of rods, and nobody to stand between them. I should like to have seen it.
Take what the beach offers: a booth in your own name, third from the water, and Dragomir's hand as a partner
Take no ground on a beach a king has marked: a partner, and a lading
Ask only for what you used: the way through the shoals behind the island

The beach gives you the plot beside Dragomir's, which makes it third from the water and his the fourth. He says nothing about that, and it is the largest gift of all. Eight cords of marten, twelve cakes of wax and eight crocks of honey, brought by forty-one households, each a little. Dragomir swears partnership over a bowl filled from the bay. The Danish king will hear a Frisian has a booth at Reric, and will draw his own conclusion.

'Wise,' says Thrasco's man. 'He came once.' Dragomir fills a bowl from the bay and swears: half his lading yours, half yours his, while both boats float. Ten cords of marten and eight cakes of wax go into your boat, and his boat follows yours out past the island the next morning.

They laugh, and load you all the same: six cords of marten and six cakes of wax. And an old Wend sits at your steering oar for a month and takes you through every gut and over every bar of the bay, at every state of the tide, until you could do it in fog. You come out of it knowing the water and most of his tongue.
The finder's share

The taking of Reric is shared out on the strand, by tally, with a scale on a tripod. The king's spokesman calls the leaders of the ships first, then the men who were useful. The Wends watch from between their rods. They have not been asked to, and nobody has told them to stop.
The Frisian who counted. Forty-one booths and nine locks, and it was as he said, to the booth. The king does not forget a true count.
There is silver, by weight. There is a Wend boat by the rods there, sound, whose owner will not be needing her to go anywhere. Choose. Not both; you are useful, you are not a ship's leader.
Or take all silver, and put your goods in my store. My man watches it day and night; he has to, for the pen. You count and I keep. We need never like each other.

I gave you bread. My wife gave you a honey cake while you were counting us. I will not swear anything about you, Frisian. I will only tell it, over water, to every Wend who comes to this strand. Water goes everywhere.
Take the Wend boat drawn up by the rods, and fifty ounces of silver
Take silver, and Asulf's offer: a corner of his store and his man to watch it
Take the silver and the king's peace, and nothing that had an owner you knew

Fifty ounces on the scale, and the boat: clinker-built of oak, pegged with wood in the Wends' way, sweet in her lines. Her owner stands between his rods and watches you run your hand along her strakes. He rowed her here himself. No Wend on the Slie will sell to you or buy from you after today.

Seventy-five ounces on the scale. Asulf shows you your corner: dry, barred, and one wall away from the pen. You can hear them through it. 'You stop noticing,' he says. No Wend on the Slie will sell to you or buy from you after today.

A little under sixty ounces, and the spokesman's word before witnesses that the Frisian's boat goes in the king's peace wherever the king's ships are. You leave the boat where she lies. It makes no difference to her owner, or to what he tells the others over water.
This year the king of the Danes burned the Wends' market at Reric, and put its merchants in his ships, and set them down at Sliesthorp.
The king of the Danes came to the Wends' market at Reric with his ships and found the booths empty. He burned them and went home. They say a stranger warned the beach.
The merchants the Danish king carried off from Reric have roofs at Sliesthorp now and a plank road to the water. There is a Frisian plot among them.
A Wend of the Slie and a Frisian shipman have sworn partnership over water. The Wend says the Frisian carried his goods out of Reric before the fire and brought back the price.
The Wends are trading at Reric again under new reed. The strand the Danish king marked out for them at Sliesthorp stands empty, and wax is dear there.

A beach market on a summer afternoon: a wide-faced Wend in a fur-edged cap sits before a stack of round wax cakes with a wax tally in his hand, a thin Saxon crouched at his shoulder; behind them sunk huts with reed roofs and boats drawn up on the sand.

Inside a sunk booth at Reric, light from the door: the Wend tries an axe edge on his thumbnail, crates of iron tools open on the floor, a bowl of water between him and the merchant; his wife, silver rings at her temples, sets down bread and honey.

A Danish strand in spring under a grey sky: a row of long hulls being tarred, shields stacked under a sail, a stout dealer with a plaited beard and a hazel switch counting coils of rope while a king's man with a spear looks straight out at us.

The beach at Reric at dusk in early summer, calm: booths, cooking fires, children catching crabs under the boats; in the foreground the Frisian and the Wend stand close and speak low, an island dark across the bay behind them.

Reric at noon in high summer: the bay crowded with striped sails and long ships, armed men carrying wax, looms and chests down to the water, the first reed roofs alight; on the rise behind, small and still, a horseman in a red cloak.
A landing on a windy autumn day: a shipman tells his news with both hands spread wide to a ring of listeners; at his feet a few cakes of wax, each with a thumbprint; grey water and one sail behind.

Evening at sea, low red light: a long line of ships going north along a flat coast, a Wend boat ahead with a loom lashed across her thwarts and a goat in the bows, a guard ship with shields along her side keeping the outside of the line.

The strand at Sliesthorp on a dull late-summer morning: two king's men stretch a knotted rope and drive hazel rods, Wendish families sit on bundles and looms waiting, a rope pen of captives to one side; up the slope a line of men with spades.

A spring morning at the jetty at Sliesthorp, mist on the water: a Dane in a clean shirt and a good cloak stands close to the merchant at the boat's side, cutting a piece from a silver arm-ring; his armed men wait out of hearing.

A timber hall at Dorestad, daylight through the door: a grey Frankish count on a bench leans forward, a tonsured clerk beside him writes on a wax tablet without looking up, the merchant stands before them cap in hand; the river and masts beyond.

Sliesthorp a year on, a bright cold morning with the ice just gone: new wattle houses in rows with their short ends to the water, a plank road, smoke from many roofs, a Frisian boat at a half-built jetty; a green earth wall along the skyline.

A low new house on the Slie, firelight: pennies counted out in fours on a board, a bowl of water between the Wend and the Frisian, the Wend's hand raised over it; his wife holds out a ring of twisted silver wire, a boy watches from the door.

The beach at Reric in clear autumn light: black burnt posts and beside them new booths under green reed, forty boats coming in from behind the island, people carrying wax ashore; a Wend and a Frisian stand at a booth third from the water.

The strand at Sliesthorp, a flat grey afternoon: a scale on a tripod heaped with cut silver, the king's spokesman holding a tally, a Wendish boat drawn up by hazel rods; between the rods a Wend stands with his arms at his sides and looks at the merchant.
